courseTitle: How IT Teams Work: Agile, Waterfall, Scrum, Kanban & Software Releases

slots.practicalActivity: Pick a real or hypothetical IT request (e.g. 'build a regional sales dashboard') and sketch it two ways: once as a 5-phase Waterfall plan (Requirements, Design, Build, Test, Release) with fixed dates, and once as three two-week Agile sprints each with its own sprint goal. Note one requirement detail that would be expensive to fix if discovered in month four of the Waterfall version.
slots.deliverable: A one-page side-by-side comparison of the same request planned as Waterfall and as Agile, plus a written note on the one detail that would be costly to change late under Waterfall.

slots.practicalActivity: Write 3-5 user stories for a hypothetical dashboard project in the 'As a [role], I want [capability], so that [benefit]' shape, each with 2 specific, checkable acceptance criteria. Assign the Product Owner, Scrum Master, and Developer roles to yourself and two imaginary teammates, then run a 5-minute mock Sprint Planning session choosing one sprint goal from your stories.
slots.deliverable: A written sprint backlog of 3-5 user stories with acceptance criteria, plus the chosen sprint goal from your mock Sprint Planning session.

slots.practicalActivity: Build a real Kanban board (Trello, a free Jira or GitHub Projects board, or a spreadsheet grid) with Backlog, To Do, In Progress, Review, and Done columns. Add the 3-5 user stories from the previous slot as cards, set a WIP limit of 2 on 'In Progress', move cards through at least 3 columns to simulate a day's work, and flag one card 'Blocked' with a reason.
slots.deliverable: A screenshot or export of the populated Kanban board showing the WIP limit on In Progress and one card explicitly marked Blocked with a stated reason.

slots.practicalActivity: Pick one user story from your backlog and write out its full Dev to QA to UAT to Production journey: a branch name for the change, a one-sentence code-review comment a teammate might leave, a QA test plan with 2 test cases (including one edge case), and a one-paragraph UAT sign-off written in the business stakeholder's own voice.
slots.deliverable: A one-page 'ticket journey' document covering all four environments (branch name, code-review note, QA test plan, UAT sign-off) for a single user story.

slots.practicalActivity: Create a free GitHub account if needed, create a new repository, and run the full workflow from the lesson: git clone, git checkout -b to create a branch, make one real change to a README file, git add, git commit -m with a specific descriptive message, git push, then open a pull request on GitHub. Add a .gitignore file that excludes one scratch file type.
slots.deliverable: A GitHub repository URL showing one open or merged pull request with a descriptive commit message, plus a working .gitignore file.

slots.practicalActivity: For the repository from the previous slot, write out a full CI/CD pipeline as a diagram or ordered list: Code Commit, Automated Tests, Build, Deploy to Staging, Deploy to Production. Then write a release checklist for one hypothetical release covering approval, monitoring, rollback plan, and release notes, and pick whichever deployment strategy (blue-green, canary, rolling, or feature flag) best fits it, with a one-sentence justification.
slots.deliverable: A written release checklist (approval, monitoring, rollback plan, release notes) plus a one-paragraph deployment-strategy choice and justification.

slots.practicalActivity: Write one continuous, 300-500 word narrative tracing a single fictional feature request through every Chapter 1 concept in order: planned as Agile or Waterfall, broken into user stories with acceptance criteria, tracked on a Kanban board with a WIP limit, pushed through Dev, QA, UAT, and Production, version-controlled in Git with a pull request, and finally released through a CI/CD pipeline with a rollback plan.
slots.deliverable: One 300-500 word written narrative that correctly and specifically uses all six Chapter 1 concepts, in the right order, for a single consistent feature request.

slots.practicalActivity: Start the lesson's Castlebridge Retail capstone: turn the sales director's one-paragraph dashboard request into user stories (revenue-by-region, revenue-by-category, automatic daily refresh), each with acceptance criteria like 'the dashboard reflects the prior day's closed sales by 7 AM with no manual steps'. Build the 5-column Kanban board (Backlog, To Do, In Progress, Review, Done) and place the stories in Backlog. Write a QA test plan for each story including the zero-sales-for-a-region edge case.
slots.deliverable: The capstone's user stories with acceptance criteria, the populated 5-column Kanban board, and a QA test plan including the zero-sales edge case — the first three items of the capstone checklist.

slots.practicalActivity: Finish the Castlebridge Retail capstone: write the one-paragraph UAT sign-off in the sales director's own voice (approving the dashboard or sending back specific feedback), write short release notes in the 'Added: ... Known limitation: ...' format, and write up how you'd handle a production incident two days after launch — which environment you'd check first, what you'd look at in the data pipeline, and what you'd tell the regional manager while still investigating.
slots.deliverable: The completed capstone package — UAT sign-off, release notes, and a production-incident response plan — closing out all six items of the capstone checklist across both lesson slots.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After finishing this course, a student can read a real IT team's board, ticket, and release process and correctly place any piece of work into its right planning framework, environment, and version-control step — the shared professional vocabulary every role in this path depends on.
